prompt: The same order was sent twice with the same Idempotency-Key. What did the second answer have that the first did not?
hint: Look at the headers of the second answer.

choices.text: A new order id, ord-1002
choices.why: Both answers carried ord-1001; no second order was created.

choices.text: idempotent-replayed: true
choices.why: Right. It marks the answer as a copy of the first.

choices.text: Status 200 instead of 201
choices.why: The replay repeats the first status, 201.

choices.text: A second charge from the stub, ch-2
choices.why: The stub saw one charge for the key; the payment stayed ch-1.

prompt: A client reuses a key from a two-seat order for a three-seat order. Why does boxoffice answer 422 instead of replaying the first answer?
hint: What would the replay tell the client?

choices.text: Because three seats of sh-101 are not available
choices.why: sh-101 had plenty of seats; the refusal is about the key.

choices.text: Because keys can be used once and are then deleted
choices.why: The key is kept and replays the same request; only a different body is refused.

choices.text: It would report three seats bought, not two
choices.why: Right. A key reused for another intention is a client defect, and saying so is safer.

choices.text: Because 422 is the status for any repeated request
choices.why: The identical repeat got 201 with idempotent-replayed.

prompt: After the order, its replay and the refused three-seat order, how many charges with the key buy-7f3a did the stub hold?
hint: Count the lines /__requests printed.

prompt: Match each answer to what a client should do with it.
hint: The first digit says who should act.

pairs.right: fix the request; never retry it as it is
slow down, honouring Retry-After when it is sent
ask the user, who may choose another card

right_distractors: retry at once, as fast as possible

prompt: Why does the backoff wait a random time up to the ceiling instead of exactly the ceiling?
hint: Think of many clients that failed at the same moment.

choices.text: So clients that failed together do not return together
choices.why: Right. That is jitter: the second wave spreads out instead of hitting the server at once.

choices.text: So a test can predict the waits exactly
choices.why: Randomness makes waits harder to predict; the test passes random: () => 1 for that reason.

choices.text: Because setTimeout cannot wait an exact number of milliseconds
choices.why: setTimeout takes a number; precision is not the reason for jitter.

choices.text: So the total wait never grows past the first ceiling
choices.why: The ceiling still doubles each try, up to the cap.

prompt: Why can withRetry's tests run in milliseconds, with no server?
hint: Look at its parameters.

choices.text: Node skips setTimeout inside node:test
choices.why: node:test runs timers as usual; the tests replace sleep instead.

choices.text: The waits are too short to notice
choices.why: Real waits of 100 to 500 ms would add up to seconds.

choices.text: fetch is never called because the helper caches answers
choices.why: The helper caches nothing; the tests pass a fake send.

choices.text: send, sleep and random are parameters the tests replace
choices.why: Right. A fake send gives statuses, a fake sleep records instead of waiting.

prompt: A waiting time whose ceiling doubles with each try is called exponential ___.
hint: The opposite of rushing back.

prompt: Which of these did the error-path tests check after a declined charge?
hint: Three things: the answer, the state, the next sale.

choices.text: The status, 402, and the problem body
choices.why: Right. The answer the client gets.

choices.text: That sh-103 still had the same seats left
choices.why: Right. The state left behind.

choices.text: That the declined order was deleted
choices.why: It was kept, with status declined; the test did not ask.

choices.text: That all four seats could be sold afterwards
choices.why: Right. The last test proves nothing was left reserved.

prompt: GET /v1/orders/ord-1003 showed an order with status failed. Why does the section call that a finding rather than only a detail?
hint: What did the 502 tell the client?

choices.text: A failed order should have held the seats
choices.why: Releasing them is right; the seats were free.

choices.text: Its id never reached the client
choices.why: Right. The 502 carried no id, which leaves reconciliation impossible.

choices.text: boxoffice should answer 404 for any failed order
choices.why: Hiding the record would not help the client either; the question is the missing id.

choices.text: The order shows the client was charged
choices.why: The provider was down; nothing was charged in that case.

prompt: A new version of boxoffice forgets to release the seats when the provider answers 500, but still answers 502. Which test in errors.test.mjs fails first?
hint: Which assertion looks at the seats right after the 502?

choices.text: decline, because it runs first
choices.why: The decline path still releases the seats; its checks hold.

choices.text: None: the status is still right, so every test passes
choices.why: Each error test also compares seats before and after.

choices.text: Only the last one, when four seats cannot be sold
choices.why: It would fail too, but the down test fails first, on its seat check.

choices.text: down, on its seats-left assertion
choices.why: Right. The status passes and the seat count does not.

prompt: Why did section 02's replay test pass, although boxoffice has the race?
hint: When did its second request start?

choices.text: Its second request started after the first had finished
choices.why: Right. By then the key was remembered; the race needs both in flight.

choices.text: Its stub was too fast for the race to show
choices.why: The stub's speed only sets the window; sequential requests never enter it.

choices.text: It used a different show from the race test
choices.why: The show plays no part; the key does.

choices.text: It had the todo option, which hides failures
choices.why: It has no todo; it passed for real.

prompt: Why does the race get worse in production than against the local stub?
hint: How long is the window?

choices.text: Production runs more copies of Node, each with its own clock
choices.why: Clocks have nothing to do with it; the window is the time the charge takes.

choices.text: A real provider takes longer, so the window is wider
choices.why: Right. The key is only remembered after the charge returns.

choices.text: Real phones send three requests on a double tap
choices.why: A double tap is two requests; the count is not the problem.

choices.text: Idempotency keys expire faster in production
choices.why: Expiry is about later replays, not requests at the same moment.

prompt: What fix does the section propose for the race?
hint: When should the key be recorded?

choices.text: Ask clients to wait two seconds before tapping again
choices.why: That moves the defect onto every app and still loses to a retry.

choices.text: Remember the key after the charge, but faster
choices.why: Any gap between checking and remembering is the window.

choices.text: Claim the key as in progress when it is checked
choices.why: Right. A second request finds it taken and waits or gets 409.

choices.text: Drop the Idempotency-Key header and rely on the provider
choices.why: The provider does not know about orders or seats; boxoffice must keep its promise.

prompt: boxoffice answered 504 after about two seconds. What does that tell you about the payment?
hint: Look at the stub's record afterwards.

choices.text: It failed, so nothing was charged
choices.why: The stub had the charge and approved it a second later.

choices.text: It succeeded, since the provider always finishes
choices.why: A provider can fail after a timeout too; the 504 does not say which.

choices.text: Nothing: its outcome is unknown
choices.why: Right. A timeout is the absence of an answer.

choices.text: That the provider is down and answered 500
choices.why: That case gave 502; this provider was slow, not down.

prompt: Why does timeout.test.mjs check that the request took at least 1.9 seconds?
hint: What would a 504 after 50 ms mean?

choices.text: An early 504 means a false deadline
choices.why: Right. The lower bound catches a deadline that fires early.

choices.text: Because node:test cannot measure anything shorter
choices.why: performance.now() measures fractions of a millisecond.

choices.text: To give the stub time to approve the charge
choices.why: The assertion measures, it does not wait; the stub takes three seconds anyway.

choices.text: Because the test's own timeout is 1.9 seconds
choices.why: The test's timeout is five seconds.

prompt: Why does the timeout test carry the option { timeout: 5000 }?
hint: What if boxoffice never answered?

choices.text: To make boxoffice give up after five seconds
choices.why: The option belongs to the test; boxoffice's deadline is its own two seconds.

choices.text: So a hung request fails the test instead of blocking the suite
choices.why: Right. A test with no limit hangs with the server.

choices.text: Because node:test refuses tests longer than two seconds
choices.why: Node has no such limit by default.

choices.text: To slow the stub down to five seconds
choices.why: MODE=slow sets the stub's delay, three seconds.

prompt: An app gets 504 from boxoffice for a purchase and shows "Payment failed, try again". What should it do instead?
hint: A 504 is not a failure.

choices.text: Retry at once with a new idempotency key, so it is not refused
choices.why: A new key makes the retry a new purchase, which is how people pay twice.

choices.text: Treat it as unknown: same key, or ask first
choices.why: Right. The charge may have gone through.

choices.text: Show success, because most slow charges are approved
choices.why: Guessing the outcome either way misleads the user.

choices.text: Never retry anything that took longer than two seconds
choices.why: 504 is one of the answers worth retrying, safely, with the same key.

prompt: Put the events of the slow-provider case in the order they happened.
hint: boxoffice gives up before the stub finishes.
items: boxoffice holds the seats and sends the charge
after two seconds boxoffice gives up and marks the order failed
the stub approves the charge, with nobody listening

prompt: Which of these are safe for withRetry to wrap?
hint: Retrying is safe only where repeating is safe.

choices.text: GET /v1/shows/sh-103
choices.why: Right. A safe method can be sent again freely.

choices.text: POST /v1/orders with the same Idempotency-Key on every try
choices.why: Right, apart from the race: a retry only starts after the previous answer arrived.

choices.text: POST /v1/orders with no Idempotency-Key
choices.why: Each retry after a 504 could create another order and another charge.

choices.text: POST /v1/orders with a new random key on each try
choices.why: A new key is a new intention, so it is the same as having none.

prompt: The provider becomes slower, often taking 1.5 seconds per charge. Which defect of this lesson becomes more frequent, and which test shows it?
hint: Which window depends on the charge's duration?

choices.text: Retries of 422, shown by retry.test.mjs
choices.why: Retrying 422 depends on the client's code, not on the provider's speed.

choices.text: Seats held after a decline, shown by errors.test.mjs
choices.why: The decline path releases seats at any speed.

choices.text: Wrong replay bodies, shown by idempotency.test.mjs
choices.why: Sequential replays stay correct whatever the provider's speed.

choices.text: The double charge, shown by race.test.mjs
choices.why: Right. The window between checking and remembering the key is the charge's duration.
